medical.title: International study validates less invasive approach to diagnosing mitochondrial disease
medical.summary: Researchers at Children's Hospital Colorado (Children's Colorado) and the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine have published one of the largest studies to date evaluating advanced laboratory testing for mitochondrial disease, providing new evidence that a small skin biopsy can often help diagnose these rare and complex conditions without the need for more invasive procedures.

medical.title: Why chronic low back pain feels 'personal'
medical.summary: Low back pain is the single leading cause of disability worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. For people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) lasting more than 12 weeks, a sudden pain flare triggered by movement can often worsen the condition. Pain signals originate in the brain, but scientists still don't fully understand the specific neural circuitry that sparks this movement-based pain.

medical.title: Before building mental health apps, designers need to understand the problem
medical.summary: When technology designers work on mental health issues that people tend to conceal or struggle to describe, they often end up with elegant solutions that can make problems worse, according to new research from the University at Buffalo School of Management.

medical.title: Cell-free treatment reduces brain damage and improves recovery after stroke in mice
medical.summary: Ischemic stroke can leave lasting neurological damage after the initial vascular event, with oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, neuronal death and disruption of neural connectivity contributing to impaired recovery. Although current interventions provide partial protection, their ability to prevent delayed neuronal injury remains limited, highlighting a major barrier to functional recovery.

medical.title: Why antidepressants can stop working after initially helping
medical.summary: Antidepressant use continues to rise. In England, 96 million antidepressant prescription items were dispensed to an estimated 9.1 million patients in 2025–2026. These medicines are prescribed for depression and other conditions, including anxiety and some forms of pain.

medical.title: Two studies link elevated ear protein levels in blood to tinnitus
medical.summary: When Dr. Kourosh Parham conceived a first-of-its-kind blood test for tinnitus, he knew further research was needed to confirm a link between a unique ear protein and the common hearing disorder. To validate his theory, the professor of surgery at UConn Health (UCH), Division of Otolaryngology-Head & Neck Surgery, teamed up with fellow UCH physician-scientists to conduct two clinical trials.

medical.title: What is a professional patient advocate, and why might you need one?
medical.summary: Imagine your mom has just been discharged from the hospital to a rehabilitation center after hip replacement surgery. She has the paperwork, the facility's address—and a long list of questions. Will her insurance cover her entire rehab stay? Does she have enough pain medication until she gets settled? Will the hospital transfer her prescriptions? Are they accurate?

medical.title: Promising nonopioid approach for reducing neuropathic pain disrupts a protein interaction
medical.summary: Understanding and treating chronic neuropathic pain has remained challenging due to its complex nature. New research from the lab of Clifford Woolf, MB, BCh, Ph.D., at Boston Children's Hospital's FM Kirby Neurobiology Center describes a novel approach for reducing pain by disrupting interactions within pain-sensing nerve cells called nociceptors.

medical.title: Brain stimulation timing may shape memory outcomes in Parkinson's patients with GBA1 mutations
medical.summary: The timing of deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery is a critical factor in preserving cognitive function for Parkinson's disease patients with a specific genetic mutation, according to a new study by an international team of researchers.

medical.title: Does your sleep tracker get it right? A neuroscientist weighs in
medical.summary: On a typical night, I go to bed wearing a tracking watch on one wrist and another type of tracker on the other wrist. Then I compare their sleep findings while I drink my morning coffee.

medical.title: Biological aging offers clues to long-term health after Fontan surgery
medical.summary: Our birthdays tell us how long we have lived, but not necessarily how our bodies are aging. Biological age reflects the condition and function of our cells and tissues, shaped by genetics, lifestyle, environment and disease. In people with chronic conditions such as cancer, kidney disease and heart disease, researchers have observed signs of aging that appear earlier than expected for a person's age. This is known as accelerated biological aging.

medical.title: Digital alerts support timely treatment decisions of critically ill cardiac patients
medical.summary: For busy health care workers, the electronic health record (EHR) can feel like an endless stream of clicks and prompts. But three Michigan Medicine studies suggest that well-designed alerts for critically ill cardiac patients can change what happens at the bedside, prompting clinicians to make recommended treatment decisions and recognize when patients are deteriorating.

medical.title: Obesity's link to lower risk of death in dementia points to likely importance of nutrition
medical.summary: People who are overweight or obese when they are diagnosed with dementia are likely to live longer than those in a normal weight range, according to a new study by Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health. The findings suggest that weight status at the time of a dementia diagnosis may provide meaningful prognostic information about survival and underscore the need for greater attention to nutrition among those with dementia.

medical.title: Childhood obesity less common under new health-based definition
medical.summary: A new global definition of clinical obesity classifies far fewer children as obese than widely used body mass index (BMI) thresholds, according to a large international study. The findings could lead to changes in how childhood obesity is identified and managed.

medical.title: How short is too short? Long-term wearable data point to a more personal way of defining insufficient sleep
medical.summary: How much sleep is enough? Public health recommendations necessarily give population-level answers. But with wearable devices now capable of recording hundreds of nights from the same person, researchers from the National University of Singapore (NUS) have asked whether short sleep could also be assessed relative to an individual's own sleep pattern.

medical.title: Minimally invasive technique offers lasting relief for carpal tunnel syndrome
medical.summary: A minimally invasive ultrasound-guided technique offers long-term relief for patients with carpal tunnel syndrome with fewer side effects than steroids, according to a new study published in Radiology.

medical.title: Do you really need to fast before every blood test? New study suggests not
medical.summary: Even a routine blood test may come with an overnight fasting requirement. Many medical practices still ask patients to go without food for 8–12 hours before blood is drawn. While the protocol was originally recommended for glucose and lipid testing, over time, it became the default requirement for almost all routine blood panels. Why it is still followed for such a broad range of routine lab tests is a question that researchers from South Korea asked in a recent study.

medical.title: Colorectal cancer is rising in young people and often found too late
medical.summary: Colorectal cancer in young people is often diagnosed at an advanced stage, with researchers finding most patients age 21 or younger already had Stage III or IV disease. Because symptoms like rectal bleeding, weight loss, abdominal pain, and bowel changes may be overlooked, researchers are calling for greater vigilance.

medical.title: Why old dogs might be able to teach Alzheimer's researchers new tricks
medical.summary: Most people know someone with Alzheimer's disease. When I was growing up, my grandmother struggled with dementia, and I saw firsthand how difficult that was for our family.

medical.title: Antimalarial drug persists in mosquitoes for days, potentially exposing developing parasites
medical.summary: Antimalarial drugs are designed to protect people from malaria, but they may also affect the mosquitoes exposed to them during blood meals. A new Yale study, published in The Journal of Infectious Diseases, investigates the impact of these medications on mosquitoes, laying the groundwork for future research into how the drugs may influence the malaria parasites developing within them.

medical.title: Goodbye joint replacements? Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis
medical.summary: Scientists have found a surprising way to regrow damaged knee cartilage by blocking a protein that becomes more abundant with age. In old mice, the treatment restored naturally lost cartilage and also helped prevent osteoarthritis after ACL-like knee injuries, while human cartilage taken from knee replacement patients began producing new, functional joint cartilage after exposure to the same inhibitor.

medical.title: Researchers looking into foundations of autoimmune disease development, may yield new treatments
medical.summary: An Idaho State University biologist and her students are exploring new ways to fight autoimmune diseases afflicting millions. "Normally, our immune system makes antibodies that target pathogens for destruction," said Kinta Serve, an associate professor at ISU. "These antibodies recognize specific pathogen molecules, like bacterial proteins, while ignoring our own host molecules.

medical.title: Even brief e-cigarette use can cause lasting lung damage and weaken defenses against respiratory viruses, study suggests
medical.summary: Just days of e-cigarette vapor exposure can injure the lungs' most delicate tissue and leave it more vulnerable to viral infection, according to a study led by National Jewish Health researchers and published in JCI Insight.

medical.title: Scientists say this simple habit could strengthen your marriage
medical.summary: Couples who exercise together report better communication, healthier conflict resolution, and lower marital stress than those who work out alone. Even something as simple as taking a walk together may create valuable opportunities to talk, listen, and feel more connected.

medical.title: Slow down, reminisce if it feels right: Practical tips for talking to people with dementia
medical.summary: No one likes to feel left out of the conversation—including people living with dementia. Sometimes, all it takes is a little extra thought to make sure everyone feels included.

science.title: Noncompetes suppress worker mobility and earnings without protecting trade secrets
science.summary: Findings recently published in The Quarterly Journal of Economics provide, according to the study's authors, the clearest cause-and-effect evidence to date that noncompete agreements reduce worker mobility and earnings—while offering no measurable benefits in protecting sensitive business information.

science.title: Did the hot summer make more people worry about climate change?
science.summary: This summer broke records around the U.K. for maximum temperatures and dry weather. According to the U.K.'s Met Office, while it was rare to hit 35°C (95°F) in the 20th century, that temperature has been surpassed in six out of the past 10 years. And temperatures are only expected to get higher.

science.title: Striking new images of unique supernova remnant reveal pearl-like chains
science.summary: The only known supernova remnant of its kind in the Milky Way has an unexpectedly intricate structure: chains of gas knots resembling pearls on a string, each wide enough to fit the solar system multiple times. Using the Gemini North telescope, an international team co-led by Ilaria Caiazzo, assistant professor at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), captured the most detailed view yet of Pa 30, revealing striking new features of the remnant associated with a historical supernova witnessed nearly 850 years ago. The findings are published in The Astrophysical Journal.

science.title: Columbus' own writings reveal how tightly religion and conquest were intertwined from the start
science.summary: Few historical figures are as divisive as Christopher Columbus. For some, in both Spain and the United States, he remains a great hero, an explorer who found a "new world." He is reviled by others who see him as an arrogant conqueror: the first European to enslave Indigenous Americans and the man who launched ecological destruction in the Western Hemisphere.

science.title: Why people keep looking for Noah's Ark in a natural rock formation in Turkey: A scholar of early Christianity explains
science.summary: A team of researchers from Sivas Cumhuriyet University in Turkey is investigating a long-standing claim: that a boat-shaped geological formation in the country's east contains the remains of Noah's Ark.

science.title: What happens when food-safety chemicals react with food?
science.summary: Following the major Cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce, consumers might assume that produce labeled "triple-washed" offers greater protection from foodborne illness. But industrial washing cannot necessarily eliminate pathogens already established on produce. At the same time, the disinfectants used during processing may react with the food itself, creating new compounds whose effects on human health are not yet fully understood.

science.title: Heavy fermions emerge at an atomic-layer interface, unlocking new ways to design quantum materials
science.summary: A research team led by the University of Osaka has directly observed, for the first time, an unusual heavy-fermion state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. Such states are closely linked to exotic quantum phenomena, including unconventional superconductivity, and the finding opens new possibilities for designing quantum materials through their interfaces.

science.title: Popular TikTok docs have big influence on Gen Z followers, new research finds
science.summary: Young adults following physicians on TikTok consider them more accessible, credible and altruistic than their own doctors, even when the physician-influencers are selling products. Moreover, the followers haven't actually confirmed the influencers' medical credentials. Those are the main findings of a new study from Virginia Commonwealth University, co-authored by Suzanne Makarem, Ph.D., and published in the Journal of Consumer Affairs.

science.title: To keep GPS constellations from drifting, look to the moon
science.summary: Global positioning systems are a key feature in everyday life for much of the world's population. Whether it's ensuring a ship delivers its goods safely or helping you avoid a road closure on your commute home, GPS can help.

science.title: A symbiotic marketplace: Gutless worms swap essential bacterial partners over time
science.summary: A typical scene at a local farmers market: Various stalls offer fruit, vegetables and much more. Every customer has their favorite stalls, though these may change occasionally. Some symbiotic relationships seem to work just like that, a study by researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Marine Microbiology reveals in Science Advances.

science.title: Can a passing black hole disturbance leave a trace in Hawking radiation?
science.summary: Black holes, despite their extreme nature, are described by surprisingly few basic parameters: their mass, charge and spin. Two black holes may have formed for completely different reasons and passed through very different histories, yet still end up in the same final state. John Wheeler summarized this idea with the famous phrase "black holes have no hair."

science.title: Bacteria use collisions to navigate crowded environments, micro-maze experiments reveal
science.summary: Some bacteria can sense when they bump into each other and use these interactions to shape how the group organizes and moves. This discovery reveals a new way microbes explore their environments using physical feedback rather than chemical signals.

science.title: AI chatbots may increase accurate political knowledge
science.summary: As voters seeking information about political issues increasingly turn to LLMs to do research, will AI lead them astray with hallucinations and bias, distorting the democratic process? Maybe not, according to a study of AI use in the 2024 U.K. election, published in PNAS Nexus.

science.title: Molecular complexity as a signature of life
science.summary: An abundance of complex molecules has been proposed as a universal signature of life.

science.title: Vanillin provides a sweet solution for chronic wound healing
science.summary: A team from Flinders University's Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory has found that vanillin has pronounced antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties, making it a good candidate for wound-healing formulations. Their work is published in the International Journal of Pharmaceutics.

science.title: Blue light could cut food poisoning from raw chicken
science.summary: A low-power blue light could be the key to significantly reducing food poisoning caused by raw chicken in the U.K., scientists at the University of Reading have found. Campylobacter is the most common cause of bacterial food poisoning worldwide. In the U.K. alone, there are hundreds of thousands of cases each year, costing an estimated £700 million annually in health care and lost productivity.

science.title: Counting purpose and connection could reveal overlooked benefits of bike paths and parks
science.summary: It's often the sight of heavy digging machinery that makes us question how our taxes and property taxes are being spent. As a new project begins, we may wonder why money is being spent on that and not on other things.

science.title: Archaeologists may have finally solved a 100-year-old Florida mystery
science.summary: Ancient pottery from Tampa Bay appears to have been made by migrant craftspeople who brought specialized Mississippian pottery-making knowledge hundreds of miles south. Remarkably, they even incorporated crushed fragments of older homeland pottery into new vessels, preserving a physical link to their past across generations.

science.title: New report exposes modern poverty and inequality in one of Britain's 'most affluent cities'
science.summary: The University of York's Cost of Living Research Group has examined modern living standards across the city and revealed the extent of hidden pockets of poverty and inequality in one of the North's most affluent cities.

science.title: Africa's rhinos often get the spotlight—but Indonesia's two rhino species are far closer to extinction
science.summary: Small, hairy and cheekily charismatic. Those words sprang to mind when I first met a Sumatran rhinoceros (Dicerorhinus sumatrensis) after traversing the maze of wooden slat paths at the conservation center in the dense, humid forests of Malaysian Borneo.

science.title: Physicists just saw quarks make waves in the Big Bang’s primordial soup
science.summary: Physicists at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider have captured the clearest evidence yet that quark-gluon plasma, the scorching-hot matter that filled the newborn universe, behaves like a true liquid. By tracking individual quarks as they blasted through the plasma, researchers saw them leave behind ripples, splashes, and swirling wakes much like a duck moving through water. The finding suggests this primordial “soup” is so dense that it can slow speeding quarks and respond collectively as a fluid.

science.title: Yosemite's meadows can be restored, but it will take time and effort
science.summary: Researchers at Colorado State University are leading an attempt to restore Yosemite National Park's iconic meadows before it's too late by reintroducing native plants that once covered the landscape. Results are published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences.

science.title: Rising heat linked to faster telomere loss in wild Australian birds
science.summary: Extreme heat can have a profound impact on wild animals, causing their death in the most extreme cases and leaving less visible marks in others. Understanding the effects of temperature changes on specific species could inform conservation efforts and other initiatives aimed at protecting natural ecosystems from climate change.

science.title: Cancer survival is improving, but return‑to‑work support is falling behind
science.summary: Australia has made significant strides in improving cancer survival, but new research from Griffith University finds far less progress in supporting survivors' return to work, which remains a major challenge for many. The industry research report, "Return-to-Work for Cancer Survivors in the Life Insurance Context," was a joint research collaboration between Griffith University and Hannover Life Re of Australasia Ltd. and was published in the Griffith Research Repository.

science.title: New report reveals gaps in corporate modern slavery disclosures
science.summary: Many of Australia's largest companies fail to show enough public evidence that workers affected by modern slavery can safely report concerns, a new Monash University–led report has found.

environment.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
environment.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

environment.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

environment.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
environment.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

environment.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
environment.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

environment.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
environment.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

environment.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
environment.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

environment.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
environment.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

environment.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
environment.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

environment.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
environment.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.summary: Protestele elevilor și studenților din Franța se extind marți, într-o „zi a mobilizării” la care s-au alăturat sindicate din educație și organizații ale părinților. mix_items.title: Noncompetes suppress worker mobility and earnings without protecting trade secrets
mix_items.summary: Findings recently published in The Quarterly Journal of Economics provide, according to the study's authors, the clearest cause-and-effect evidence to date that noncompete agreements reduce worker mobility and earnings—while offering no measurable benefits in protecting sensitive business information.

mix_items.title: International study validates less invasive approach to diagnosing mitochondrial disease
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Children's Hospital Colorado (Children's Colorado) and the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine have published one of the largest studies to date evaluating advanced laboratory testing for mitochondrial disease, providing new evidence that a small skin biopsy can often help diagnose these rare and complex conditions without the need for more invasive procedures.

mix_items.title: Did the hot summer make more people worry about climate change?
mix_items.summary: This summer broke records around the U.K. for maximum temperatures and dry weather. According to the U.K.'s Met Office, while it was rare to hit 35°C (95°F) in the 20th century, that temperature has been surpassed in six out of the past 10 years. And temperatures are only expected to get higher.

mix_items.title: Striking new images of unique supernova remnant reveal pearl-like chains
mix_items.summary: The only known supernova remnant of its kind in the Milky Way has an unexpectedly intricate structure: chains of gas knots resembling pearls on a string, each wide enough to fit the solar system multiple times. Using the Gemini North telescope, an international team co-led by Ilaria Caiazzo, assistant professor at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), captured the most detailed view yet of Pa 30, revealing striking new features of the remnant associated with a historical supernova witnessed nearly 850 years ago. The findings are published in The Astrophysical Journal.

mix_items.title: Why chronic low back pain feels 'personal'
mix_items.summary: Low back pain is the single leading cause of disability worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. For people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) lasting more than 12 weeks, a sudden pain flare triggered by movement can often worsen the condition. Pain signals originate in the brain, but scientists still don't fully understand the specific neural circuitry that sparks this movement-based pain.

mix_items.title: Before building mental health apps, designers need to understand the problem
mix_items.summary: When technology designers work on mental health issues that people tend to conceal or struggle to describe, they often end up with elegant solutions that can make problems worse, according to new research from the University at Buffalo School of Management.

mix_items.title: Columbus' own writings reveal how tightly religion and conquest were intertwined from the start
mix_items.summary: Few historical figures are as divisive as Christopher Columbus. For some, in both Spain and the United States, he remains a great hero, an explorer who found a "new world." He is reviled by others who see him as an arrogant conqueror: the first European to enslave Indigenous Americans and the man who launched ecological destruction in the Western Hemisphere.

mix_items.title: Cell-free treatment reduces brain damage and improves recovery after stroke in mice
mix_items.summary: Ischemic stroke can leave lasting neurological damage after the initial vascular event, with oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, neuronal death and disruption of neural connectivity contributing to impaired recovery. Although current interventions provide partial protection, their ability to prevent delayed neuronal injury remains limited, highlighting a major barrier to functional recovery.

mix_items.title: Why antidepressants can stop working after initially helping
mix_items.summary: Antidepressant use continues to rise. In England, 96 million antidepressant prescription items were dispensed to an estimated 9.1 million patients in 2025–2026. These medicines are prescribed for depression and other conditions, including anxiety and some forms of pain.

mix_items.title: Two studies link elevated ear protein levels in blood to tinnitus
mix_items.summary: When Dr. Kourosh Parham conceived a first-of-its-kind blood test for tinnitus, he knew further research was needed to confirm a link between a unique ear protein and the common hearing disorder. To validate his theory, the professor of surgery at UConn Health (UCH), Division of Otolaryngology-Head & Neck Surgery, teamed up with fellow UCH physician-scientists to conduct two clinical trials.

mix_items.title: What is a professional patient advocate, and why might you need one?
mix_items.summary: Imagine your mom has just been discharged from the hospital to a rehabilitation center after hip replacement surgery. She has the paperwork, the facility's address—and a long list of questions. Will her insurance cover her entire rehab stay? Does she have enough pain medication until she gets settled? Will the hospital transfer her prescriptions? Are they accurate?

mix_items.title: Why people keep looking for Noah's Ark in a natural rock formation in Turkey: A scholar of early Christianity explains
mix_items.summary: A team of researchers from Sivas Cumhuriyet University in Turkey is investigating a long-standing claim: that a boat-shaped geological formation in the country's east contains the remains of Noah's Ark.

mix_items.title: What happens when food-safety chemicals react with food?
mix_items.summary: Following the major Cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce, consumers might assume that produce labeled "triple-washed" offers greater protection from foodborne illness. But industrial washing cannot necessarily eliminate pathogens already established on produce. At the same time, the disinfectants used during processing may react with the food itself, creating new compounds whose effects on human health are not yet fully understood.

mix_items.title: Heavy fermions emerge at an atomic-layer interface, unlocking new ways to design quantum materials
mix_items.summary: A research team led by the University of Osaka has directly observed, for the first time, an unusual heavy-fermion state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. Such states are closely linked to exotic quantum phenomena, including unconventional superconductivity, and the finding opens new possibilities for designing quantum materials through their interfaces.

mix_items.title: Popular TikTok docs have big influence on Gen Z followers, new research finds
mix_items.summary: Young adults following physicians on TikTok consider them more accessible, credible and altruistic than their own doctors, even when the physician-influencers are selling products. Moreover, the followers haven't actually confirmed the influencers' medical credentials. Those are the main findings of a new study from Virginia Commonwealth University, co-authored by Suzanne Makarem, Ph.D., and published in the Journal of Consumer Affairs.

mix_items.title: Promising nonopioid approach for reducing neuropathic pain disrupts a protein interaction
mix_items.summary: Understanding and treating chronic neuropathic pain has remained challenging due to its complex nature. New research from the lab of Clifford Woolf, MB, BCh, Ph.D., at Boston Children's Hospital's FM Kirby Neurobiology Center describes a novel approach for reducing pain by disrupting interactions within pain-sensing nerve cells called nociceptors.

mix_items.title: Brain stimulation timing may shape memory outcomes in Parkinson's patients with GBA1 mutations
mix_items.summary: The timing of deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery is a critical factor in preserving cognitive function for Parkinson's disease patients with a specific genetic mutation, according to a new study by an international team of researchers.

mix_items.title: Does your sleep tracker get it right? A neuroscientist weighs in
mix_items.summary: On a typical night, I go to bed wearing a tracking watch on one wrist and another type of tracker on the other wrist. Then I compare their sleep findings while I drink my morning coffee.

mix_items.title: To keep GPS constellations from drifting, look to the moon
mix_items.summary: Global positioning systems are a key feature in everyday life for much of the world's population. Whether it's ensuring a ship delivers its goods safely or helping you avoid a road closure on your commute home, GPS can help.

mix_items.title: Biological aging offers clues to long-term health after Fontan surgery
mix_items.summary: Our birthdays tell us how long we have lived, but not necessarily how our bodies are aging. Biological age reflects the condition and function of our cells and tissues, shaped by genetics, lifestyle, environment and disease. In people with chronic conditions such as cancer, kidney disease and heart disease, researchers have observed signs of aging that appear earlier than expected for a person's age. This is known as accelerated biological aging.

mix_items.title: Digital alerts support timely treatment decisions of critically ill cardiac patients
mix_items.summary: For busy health care workers, the electronic health record (EHR) can feel like an endless stream of clicks and prompts. But three Michigan Medicine studies suggest that well-designed alerts for critically ill cardiac patients can change what happens at the bedside, prompting clinicians to make recommended treatment decisions and recognize when patients are deteriorating.

mix_items.title: Obesity's link to lower risk of death in dementia points to likely importance of nutrition
mix_items.summary: People who are overweight or obese when they are diagnosed with dementia are likely to live longer than those in a normal weight range, according to a new study by Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health. The findings suggest that weight status at the time of a dementia diagnosis may provide meaningful prognostic information about survival and underscore the need for greater attention to nutrition among those with dementia.

mix_items.title: A symbiotic marketplace: Gutless worms swap essential bacterial partners over time
mix_items.summary: A typical scene at a local farmers market: Various stalls offer fruit, vegetables and much more. Every customer has their favorite stalls, though these may change occasionally. Some symbiotic relationships seem to work just like that, a study by researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Marine Microbiology reveals in Science Advances.

mix_items.title: Childhood obesity less common under new health-based definition
mix_items.summary: A new global definition of clinical obesity classifies far fewer children as obese than widely used body mass index (BMI) thresholds, according to a large international study. The findings could lead to changes in how childhood obesity is identified and managed.

mix_items.title: How short is too short? Long-term wearable data point to a more personal way of defining insufficient sleep
mix_items.summary: How much sleep is enough? Public health recommendations necessarily give population-level answers. But with wearable devices now capable of recording hundreds of nights from the same person, researchers from the National University of Singapore (NUS) have asked whether short sleep could also be assessed relative to an individual's own sleep pattern.

mix_items.title: Minimally invasive technique offers lasting relief for carpal tunnel syndrome
mix_items.summary: A minimally invasive ultrasound-guided technique offers long-term relief for patients with carpal tunnel syndrome with fewer side effects than steroids, according to a new study published in Radiology.

mix_items.title: Do you really need to fast before every blood test? New study suggests not
mix_items.summary: Even a routine blood test may come with an overnight fasting requirement. Many medical practices still ask patients to go without food for 8–12 hours before blood is drawn. While the protocol was originally recommended for glucose and lipid testing, over time, it became the default requirement for almost all routine blood panels. Why it is still followed for such a broad range of routine lab tests is a question that researchers from South Korea asked in a recent study.

mix_items.title: Can a passing black hole disturbance leave a trace in Hawking radiation?
mix_items.summary: Black holes, despite their extreme nature, are described by surprisingly few basic parameters: their mass, charge and spin. Two black holes may have formed for completely different reasons and passed through very different histories, yet still end up in the same final state. John Wheeler summarized this idea with the famous phrase "black holes have no hair."

mix_items.title: Bacteria use collisions to navigate crowded environments, micro-maze experiments reveal
mix_items.summary: Some bacteria can sense when they bump into each other and use these interactions to shape how the group organizes and moves. This discovery reveals a new way microbes explore their environments using physical feedback rather than chemical signals.

mix_items.title: AI chatbots may increase accurate political knowledge
mix_items.summary: As voters seeking information about political issues increasingly turn to LLMs to do research, will AI lead them astray with hallucinations and bias, distorting the democratic process? Maybe not, according to a study of AI use in the 2024 U.K. election, published in PNAS Nexus.

mix_items.title: Molecular complexity as a signature of life
mix_items.summary: An abundance of complex molecules has been proposed as a universal signature of life.

mix_items.title: Colorectal cancer is rising in young people and often found too late
mix_items.summary: Colorectal cancer in young people is often diagnosed at an advanced stage, with researchers finding most patients age 21 or younger already had Stage III or IV disease. Because symptoms like rectal bleeding, weight loss, abdominal pain, and bowel changes may be overlooked, researchers are calling for greater vigilance.

mix_items.title: Why old dogs might be able to teach Alzheimer's researchers new tricks
mix_items.summary: Most people know someone with Alzheimer's disease. When I was growing up, my grandmother struggled with dementia, and I saw firsthand how difficult that was for our family.

mix_items.title: Vanillin provides a sweet solution for chronic wound healing
mix_items.summary: A team from Flinders University's Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory has found that vanillin has pronounced antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties, making it a good candidate for wound-healing formulations. Their work is published in the International Journal of Pharmaceutics.

mix_items.title: Antimalarial drug persists in mosquitoes for days, potentially exposing developing parasites
mix_items.summary: Antimalarial drugs are designed to protect people from malaria, but they may also affect the mosquitoes exposed to them during blood meals. A new Yale study, published in The Journal of Infectious Diseases, investigates the impact of these medications on mosquitoes, laying the groundwork for future research into how the drugs may influence the malaria parasites developing within them.

mix_items.title: Goodbye joint replacements? Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found a surprising way to regrow damaged knee cartilage by blocking a protein that becomes more abundant with age. In old mice, the treatment restored naturally lost cartilage and also helped prevent osteoarthritis after ACL-like knee injuries, while human cartilage taken from knee replacement patients began producing new, functional joint cartilage after exposure to the same inhibitor.

mix_items.title: Researchers looking into foundations of autoimmune disease development, may yield new treatments
mix_items.summary: An Idaho State University biologist and her students are exploring new ways to fight autoimmune diseases afflicting millions. "Normally, our immune system makes antibodies that target pathogens for destruction," said Kinta Serve, an associate professor at ISU. "These antibodies recognize specific pathogen molecules, like bacterial proteins, while ignoring our own host molecules.

mix_items.title: Blue light could cut food poisoning from raw chicken
mix_items.summary: A low-power blue light could be the key to significantly reducing food poisoning caused by raw chicken in the U.K., scientists at the University of Reading have found. Campylobacter is the most common cause of bacterial food poisoning worldwide. In the U.K. alone, there are hundreds of thousands of cases each year, costing an estimated £700 million annually in health care and lost productivity.

mix_items.title: Even brief e-cigarette use can cause lasting lung damage and weaken defenses against respiratory viruses, study suggests
mix_items.summary: Just days of e-cigarette vapor exposure can injure the lungs' most delicate tissue and leave it more vulnerable to viral infection, according to a study led by National Jewish Health researchers and published in JCI Insight.

mix_items.title: Counting purpose and connection could reveal overlooked benefits of bike paths and parks
mix_items.summary: It's often the sight of heavy digging machinery that makes us question how our taxes and property taxes are being spent. As a new project begins, we may wonder why money is being spent on that and not on other things.

mix_items.title: Archaeologists may have finally solved a 100-year-old Florida mystery
mix_items.summary: Ancient pottery from Tampa Bay appears to have been made by migrant craftspeople who brought specialized Mississippian pottery-making knowledge hundreds of miles south. Remarkably, they even incorporated crushed fragments of older homeland pottery into new vessels, preserving a physical link to their past across generations.

mix_items.title: New report exposes modern poverty and inequality in one of Britain's 'most affluent cities'
mix_items.summary: The University of York's Cost of Living Research Group has examined modern living standards across the city and revealed the extent of hidden pockets of poverty and inequality in one of the North's most affluent cities.

mix_items.title: Scientists say this simple habit could strengthen your marriage
mix_items.summary: Couples who exercise together report better communication, healthier conflict resolution, and lower marital stress than those who work out alone. Even something as simple as taking a walk together may create valuable opportunities to talk, listen, and feel more connected.

mix_items.title: Africa's rhinos often get the spotlight—but Indonesia's two rhino species are far closer to extinction
mix_items.summary: Small, hairy and cheekily charismatic. Those words sprang to mind when I first met a Sumatran rhinoceros (Dicerorhinus sumatrensis) after traversing the maze of wooden slat paths at the conservation center in the dense, humid forests of Malaysian Borneo.

mix_items.title: Physicists just saw quarks make waves in the Big Bang’s primordial soup
mix_items.summary: Physicists at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider have captured the clearest evidence yet that quark-gluon plasma, the scorching-hot matter that filled the newborn universe, behaves like a true liquid. By tracking individual quarks as they blasted through the plasma, researchers saw them leave behind ripples, splashes, and swirling wakes much like a duck moving through water. The finding suggests this primordial “soup” is so dense that it can slow speeding quarks and respond collectively as a fluid.

mix_items.title: Slow down, reminisce if it feels right: Practical tips for talking to people with dementia
mix_items.summary: No one likes to feel left out of the conversation—including people living with dementia. Sometimes, all it takes is a little extra thought to make sure everyone feels included.

mix_items.title: Yosemite's meadows can be restored, but it will take time and effort
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Colorado State University are leading an attempt to restore Yosemite National Park's iconic meadows before it's too late by reintroducing native plants that once covered the landscape. Results are published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences.

mix_items.title: Rising heat linked to faster telomere loss in wild Australian birds
mix_items.summary: Extreme heat can have a profound impact on wild animals, causing their death in the most extreme cases and leaving less visible marks in others. Understanding the effects of temperature changes on specific species could inform conservation efforts and other initiatives aimed at protecting natural ecosystems from climate change.

mix_items.title: Cancer survival is improving, but return‑to‑work support is falling behind
mix_items.summary: Australia has made significant strides in improving cancer survival, but new research from Griffith University finds far less progress in supporting survivors' return to work, which remains a major challenge for many. The industry research report, "Return-to-Work for Cancer Survivors in the Life Insurance Context," was a joint research collaboration between Griffith University and Hannover Life Re of Australasia Ltd. and was published in the Griffith Research Repository.

mix_items.title: New report reveals gaps in corporate modern slavery disclosures
mix_items.summary: Many of Australia's largest companies fail to show enough public evidence that workers affected by modern slavery can safely report concerns, a new Monash University–led report has found.

mix_items.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
mix_items.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

mix_items.title: In Nepal, women seek ownership rights to the lands they tend
mix_items.summary: POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. It’s […]

mix_items.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
mix_items.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

mix_items.title: ‘Lost’ bird reappears in West Africa’s forests after more than a decade
mix_items.summary: When Paulo Ditzel first laid eyes on the bird, he knew he’d seen something special: a vibrant orange body with yellow and black wings and tail feathers, topped by a dark head set off by almost-whimsical splashes of copper on its cheek. “My brain registered, it’s the Ghana cuckooshrike,” Ditzel, a field research fellow with […]

mix_items.title: Biodiversity credits shouldn’t copy the carbon market playbook (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon […]

mix_items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
mix_items.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

mix_items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
mix_items.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific
mix_items.summary: The Pacific was buzzing with storms while the Atlantic was notably quiet. The post A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific appeared first on NASA Science .
